AN "EVENING OF SONG AND STORV"
To
celebrate Psi Upsilon's 117th Found
ers' Day, Brothers from twenty-nine
Chapters gathered for an
"Evening of
Song and Story" at the home of the BrownDartmouth-Princeton Clubs, in New York
City, on the evening of December the
eighth. Many of the Brothers, before com
ing to the gathering, took the opportunity
to have dinner with a relative, delegation
or
Chapter Brother, or friend in Psi U.
When the meeting was called to order at
8:45 P.M., the spacious dining hall of this
fine club was filled to
overflowing.
A volunteer committee headed by S.
Spencer Scott, Phi '14, assisted by cochairmen Richard M. Ross, Lambda '20,
Hon. Edwin L Garvin, Delta '97
Guest, of Honor at the New York Founders' Day
Celebration
Robert P. Hughes, Delta '20, Franklin F.
Bruder, Theta '25, and Peter A. GaBauer,
Pi '25, did a bit of pioneering in the type
of evening that was
presented. It was an
attempt to bring together old and new
Brothers for an
inexpensive evening of
good fellowship. The older group was
headed by Earl D. Babst, Iota-Phi '93,
past president of the Executive Council,
and LeRoy J. Weed, Theta '01, present
President of the Council. The younger
group had eleven members from the Eta
Chapter, between the classes of 1945
thi-ough 1949. At least half of the Brothers
present came in the years between 1940
and 1953.
In the earlier decades of this century.
Brethren would take dinner at home, and
then go out for an
evening gathering of
song, story and convivial conversation. To
attest to the success of the committee's
plans, it was
unanimously approved that
a similar party be held in the Spring of
1951, probably late in April. Please mark
your calendar, now! Notices will follow in
The Diamond, and by mail.
The presiding officer for the gathering
was S. Spencer Scott, Phi '14, who spoke
briefly about the program. He then intro
duced Alfred (Doc) H. Morton, Omicron
'19, who acted as master of ceremonies.
"Doc" is well known to legions of Psi U's,
having been a member of the Executive
Council for years; he continues his active
interest as a member of the Board of Gov
ernors of the Alumni Association. He drew
on his broad experience in the entertain
ment world, as well as his fine story telling
ability, to keep things moving at a
rapid
and delightful pace.
Our indefatigable Editor of The
Diamond, Edward C. Peattie, Phi '06,
spoke briefly about The Diamond, and
asked for some volunteers to help with
the writing and editing of our
quarterly.
This appeal, we
might add, is not local
ized!
While the singing was a
happy part of
the evening and continued on into the late
hours, we missed many members of the
University Glee Club, who could not be
present. Under the leadership of David W.
Avery, Pi '41, these glee club members
plan to have a double quartet for the
Spring party. We may have the privilege
of having the musical director of our Fra
ternity, Reinald Werrenrath, Delta '05,
with us at that time if he is not on
tour.
The highlight of the evening came when

Brother Morton so
fittingly introduced the
guest of honor, the Honorable Edwin L.
Garvin, Delta '97, the first president of the
Psi Upsilon Alumni Association. ( It should
be noted that Brother Garvin was
very
much touched by the fine turnout of Delta
men, and especially that so
many of the
Delta undergraduates were
present, to pay
him honor.) Brother Garvin told some
wonderful anecdotes�and then gave a
very
moving address, which follows:
"From ocean to ocean, north and south
of the Canadian border, Psi Upsilon
gathers tonight to celebrate Founders' Day.
This is in accord with a tradition of nearly
six score
years during which the little
group of seven Founders, whose memory
we honor, has grovwi to a
mighty company
now
numbering more than 28,000 Broth
ers, past and present, with Chapters at 30
Colleges and Universities.
"The memory of those Founders we
shall cherish with a
gratitude that cannot
be adequately expressed in words, spoken
or written. Upon all of us, I venture to
say, our
Fraternity, which they gave to us,
has had a
profound influence. With Psi
Upsilon are associated many of life's choic
est memories. To Psi Upsilon we owe
much that is rightfully considered alto
gether worth while. I like to believe that
the Founders visualized the true signifi
cance of Psi Upsilon, however, as
being not
what it brings to her sons but the effect
that it has upon their lives, disclosed by
their attitude toward others. Only if and
when we
give more than we receive do we
attain what I believe the Founders had in
mind when they chose our motto, words
never uttered abroad, nor
penned, but in
delibly engraved on the heart of every
member of our brotherhood from the mo
ment he first heard them as he made his
pledge at the shrine.
"These are solemn words, fitting, I hope,
to the occasion. But there is another side
to this celebration. Today and every
Founders' Day is an occasion of great re
joicing; it is the Birthday of Psi Upsilon,
when all her sons come together, some
here, others in many meeting places, to
pay her tribute, to pledge anew their
loyalty.
"It is not strange that Psi Upsilon has
imparted to her sons a
deep sense of re
sponsibility that is reflected in the leader
ship which she has supplied during all
these years, and today as well; in war and
in peace, in literally every field of human
activity, politics, business, the professions,
art, literature, science, to mention but a
few, Psi Upsilon men have held high
places. Not all of our brotherhood have
been prominent but a vast number have
succeeded if we measure success in the
words of one of the great men of this
century. He said, 'And I have come to
believe,�that perhaps to be wholly suc
cessful is no
part of our
problem. But to
choose successfully a
right object to aim at
�that is essential: And if we have done
that�and devoted to it all our
powers�
perhaps when we come to die, we shall
know there is on this earth no
higher form
of success.'
"When we
part, at the end of this happy
evening, we shall go our various ways, all
of us, with a renewed sense of our
obliga
tion to be sure that the standards of broth
erly love, of loyalty and of unselfishness
which were established well over a
century
ago and have been continued these many
years are maintained during what may
well be some of the most trying times in
global history. If it is the will of Divine
Providence that crises arise, Psi Upsilon,
please God, as in the past, will do her
share to make this a better world in which
to live. To do less would be to confess unworthiness to succeed to the rich heritage
of useful achievement that is ours, made
possible by those founding fathers whose
memory we celebrate tonight.
"The uncertainty of hfe does not permit
us to know what is ahead. This has been
decreed by an All Wise Providence. Most
of you are
likely to live for many years.
Some of us may be looking at each other
for the last time. As I grow older I find
that I am not sure of too many things.
But of this I am certain. When that day
comes
upon which each of us
passes from
time into eternity, he wfll realize, as never
before, that one of his most precious pos
sessions is the Diamond of Psi Upsilon that
has brought us
together tonight."

NEW MEMBER OF THE EXECUTIVE COUNCIL
DONALD
B. DERBY, Pi '18, was
elected a Member of the Executive
Council of Psi Upsilon Fraternity recently
to fill the unexpired tenn of Brother Albert
C. Jacobs, Phi '21, resigned.
Brother Derby was born in Syracuse,
New York, on
February 24, 1896, and was
educated in the Syracuse public schools.
He graduated from Central High School
in that city. He attended the New York
State College of Forestry at Syracuse Uni
versity, but was called to duty with the
United States Navy in World War I prior
to graduation.
It is fitting that Brother Derby should
be selected for this high office in the Fra
ternity that he has served so well through
the years. He has devoted untiring time
and effort toward his own Pi Chapter at
Syracuse University. At the present time,
he is serving his third term as President of
its Psi Upsilon Trust Association�the
Chapter's governing body. In addition to
these duties, during the past year he
served as Finance Committee Chairman of
the 117th Annual Fraternity Convention,
which was
coupled with the Pi Chapter's
75th Anniversary in June at Syracuse. It
was
through Brother Derby's efforts that
this Convention enjoyed such financial
success.
Until recently, he was President and
Treasurer of the Eastwood Lumber Co.,
Inc., in Syracuse, New York. The yards,
offices and buildings, except the mill, have
been leased for a
long term to the PlunkettWebster Lumber Company of New York
and New Rochelle for an
expansion of
wholesale lumber distribution in central
New York. However, a new firm has been
established under the name of The Derby
Company for the manufacture of wooden
shipping boxes, crates and other containers.
This is an
expansion of a business estab
lished during World War II by Brother
Donald B. Derby, Pi '18
Recently Elected to the Executive Council
Derby. He is also President of the Floor
Contracting Co., Inc., of Syracuse, New
York, which is engaged in the installation
of wooden ffooring.
His other business activities include be
ing Chairman of the Board of the United
States Finishing Corporation, which has
plants in Norwich and Sterling, Connecti
cut, Providence, Rhode Island, and Hartsville. South Carohna. In addition, he is a
member of the Board of Directors of both
Sativa Corporation of New York City,
which is engaged in the manufacture and
development of a new
synthetic textile
fiber, and of Reserve Supply of Central
New York, Inc., of Syracuse, which is in
the lumber field.
Brother Derby resides in Syracuse and
is the father of Brother Robert Derby, Xi
'51.

PSI U MAKES WESLEYAN COMMENCE
MENT NOTEWORTHY
A
SUCCESSFUL college is but the
fruits of its loyal and devoted
alumni. Throughout its almost 120 years,
Wesleyan University at Middletown, Con
necticut has been especially fortunate in
the high cahbre of the Brothers in the Xi
Chapter of Psi Upsilon, founded in 1843.
For many years, the Chapter's living
alumni have averaged over 600, and their
contributions to the welfare of Wesleyan
are
beyond counting in time, money and
personal equations.
It was no
surprise, therefore, to see the
August, 1950, issue of The Wesleyan Uni
versity Alumnus highlighted in word and
picture by the older and younger men of
the Xi.
At the Board meeting, Saturday morning
of Commencement week-end. Earl P.
Stevenson, '16, was elected President of
the Board of Trustees, of which he had
been Vice-President and long time
member.
Later at the Alumni luncheon, Robert
I. Laggren, '13, a Trustee of Wesleyan
and a member of the Executive Council
of Psi Upsilon, made his report as Alumni
Fund Chairman (yes, the largest amount
yet received, a result of previous ex
perience as chairman during 1935-39, and
following the chairmanships of other Xi
Brothers-C. Everett Bacon, '13, Harold
G. Travis, '20, and Robert W. Parsons '22).
Charles B. Stone, Xi '23, chairman of
the alumni association, presented Brother
Laggren with an
engrossed testimonial for
his outstanding success on the Alumni
Fund (see picture) and is several times
pictured in the Alumnus, presenting cups,
giving greetings and presiding over various
alumni gatherings.

vention in 1915; special representative of the

eral of the Philippine Islands, 1927-29. He

armament Conference, 1932.
During the first World War Brother Stim
son served with the American Expeditionary
Force in France, as a Lieutenant Colonel with

in 1891, and had been a member of the firm
of Winthrop and Stimson since 1901. He
was a member of the American, New York

clubs included the Century, University, Re
publican and Down Town Clubs of New

privately at his Long Island home, the "After
word" to the memoirs which Brother Stimson
wrote three years ago was
quoted. Time
wrote of this: "The will he left was businessfike, but he had already written a final testa
ment. . . -. It bequeathed a faith for his unpeaceful times:"
Neither a man nor a nation can live
in the past. We can
go only once
along a
given path of time, and we can
only face
in one direction, forward. . . .

the peoples and nations of the world have
made many terrible mistakes; it is a sad
thing that more than half of such a book
as this should have to be devoted to the
problem of warmaking. Yet even so, it is
weU also to reflect how much worse the
state of mankind would be if the victorious
peoples in each of the two world wars had
not been willing to undergo the sacrifices
which were the price of victory. I have
always believed that the long view of man's
history will show that his destiny on earth
is progress toward the good Iffe, even
though that progress is based on sacrifices
and sufferings which taken by themselves
seem to constitute a hideous melange of
evils.

ourselves be engulfed in the passing waves
which obscure the current of progress. The
sinfulness and weakness of man are evident
to anyone who lives in the active world.

and wise. Honor begets honor; trust
begets
trust; faith begets faith; and hope is the
mainspring of life. I have lived with the
reality of war, and I have praised soldiers;
but the hope of honorable faithful peace
is a
greater thing and I have lived with
that, too. That a man must live with both
together is inherent in the nature of our
present stormy stage of human progress,
but it has also many times been the na
ture of progress in the past, and it is not
reason for despair.
I think . . . that the people of the world
and particularly our own American people
are
strong and sound in heart. We have
been late in meeting danger, but not too
late. We have been wrong but not basically
wicked.
Those who read this book will mostly
be . . . men of the generations who must
bear the active part in the work ahead. . . .
Let them charge us with our failures and
do better in their turn. But let them not
turn aside from what they have to do, nor
think that criticism excuses inaction . . .
and let them believe in mankind and its
future, for there is good as well as evil,
and the man who tries to work for the
good, believing in its eventual victory,
while he may suffer setback and even dis
aster, will never know defeat. . . .

One of the country's outstanding small

Dr. James M. Yard, Xi '05, died on
August
3, 1950, in Danbury, Conn., Hospital at the
age of 70. His home was in Chicago, but he
had been spending the summer at his family
home in Brookfield Center, Conn.
In accordance to Brother Yard's wish to
be of service even in death, his body was
given to Yale University for research. He died
of cancer.
Born in Farmingdale, N.J., Dr. Yard was
educated at Princeton and Wesleyan Univer
sities and Hartford Theological Seminary. In
1910 he was ordained Elder in the Methodist
Episcopal Church and went to China for the
board of foreign missions of that church.
From 1910 to 1922 he was
engaged in edu
cational and church work in Chengtu, West
China. There he served as district superin
tendent of schools and churches and was a
member of the faculty of West China Union
University.
From 1922 to 1925 he was stationed in
Shanghai as editor of The China Christian
Advocate and director of world service for the
Methodist Church in China. He was a dele
gate to the general conference of the Japan
Methodist Church in 1924.
Upon his return to the United States in
1925, Brother Yard served as field representa
tive of West China Union University until
1928. From 1928 to 1933 he was director of
religion and a member of the department of
political science of Northwestern University
and from 1933 to 1935 was
secretary of die
Chicago commission . for the Defense of Hu
man
Rights.
He was Midwest director emeritus of the
National Conference of Christians and Jews.
He became director of the Chicago office of
the national conference when it opened in
1935. As Midwest director he also opened
offices in Denver, Des Moines, South Bend,
Duluth, Milwaukee, Minneapolis, Omaha and
St Louis. He retired from the post in 1948,
but continued to serve the conference in a
consultative capacity in Chicago, Minneapofis,
and Miami. At his retirement from active
service, the Chicago City Council declared
October 17 to be James M. Yard Day. A reso
lution adopted by the Council asserted that
Dr. Yard had "devoted himself tirelessly to
improving the relations of men
by helping
Chicagoans learn the true meaning of the
brotherhood of man under the fatherhood of
God."
Surviving are his widow, four daughters
and eleven grandchildren.
